analysis.one_liner: Gives workers stronger tools to recover unpaid wages and creates new penalties for wage theft.
analysis.headline: The Wage Theft Prevention and Wage Recovery Act died in the House Education and Workforce Committee without a hearing or vote; it had 18 cosponsors, all Democrats.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would create a federal right to full agreed-upon compensation for all work performed, require employers to give workers detailed pay stubs and final pay within 14 days of leaving a job, and let workers inspect their own payroll records. It would increase damages workers can recover, extend the time limit to sue for stolen wages from 2-3 years to 4-5 years, raise civil fines for repeat violators, and make it harder for employers to force workers into arbitration. It would also fund a $50 million annual grant program so community organizations and state agencies can help workers understand and enforce their rights.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-wage workers who are shortchanged on pay — including workers not paid the minimum wage, denied overtime, forced to work off the clock, or misclassified as contractors. The bill's findings note women, immigrants, and Black workers are disproportionately affected. Honest employers who already pay their workers correctly would also face less competition from violators.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-wage workers victimized by wage theft

how_it_helps.text: Creates a federal right to the full wage rate agreed to in an employment contract, not just the legal minimum, so workers can recover everything they were promised [S2].
Requires employers to provide itemized pay stubs showing hours, rates, and deductions, and to pay all final wages within 14 days of employment ending, with daily pay penalties for late payment [S2].

Raises liquidated damages from an equal amount of stolen wages to 2-3 times the amount, adds interest, extends the statute of limitations from 2-3 years to 4-5 years, and suspends the clock while the Labor Department investigates [S2].
Bars employers from forcing workers to waive their right to sue in court through pre-dispute arbitration agreements, for wage claims under this law [S2].

Raises civil fines to up to $22,030 per employee per violation, and up to $110,150 for repeat or willful violators, and requires mandatory criminal referral for record-falsifying repeat offenders [S2].

Authorizes $50 million per year through 2027 in grants to community organizations, legal aid groups, and state agencies to educate workers, help file claims, and partner with Labor Department enforcement [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers who violate wage and hour laws — businesses that underpay workers, misclassify employees as contractors, or fail to pay overtime — would face higher damages, interest, steeper fines, and mandatory criminal referrals for willful record falsification. All employers in covered industries would bear new paystub and disclosure compliance costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers violating wage and hour laws

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs would fall on all covered employers, not just violators: the bill requires hiring notices in the worker's primary language, detailed pay stubs with more than a dozen data points, and copies of payroll records within 21 days of any employee request [S2].

Higher damages and fines could drive more litigation against small businesses, including ones with genuine payroll mistakes, and the broadened presumption in favor of workers' testimony when records are incomplete shifts the burden of proof to employers in those cases [S2].

The grant program sends $50 million a year to outside organizations including labor unions to monitor employers and assist enforcement, which business groups would view as funding private parties to act as enforcers against them [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protections — full contractual pay, timely pay stubs and final pay, longer time to sue, and real penalties for repeat offenders — target practices that the bill's own findings estimate cost workers more than $15 billion a year. The costs fall mainly on violating employers, though compliant small businesses would take on real paperwork burdens and higher litigation exposure. The bill is one-sided toward workers; an honest reading is that the anti-arbitration provision and triple damages are aggressive, but the compliance cost of honest paystubs is modest compared to what wage theft costs workers and taxpayers in lost revenue.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee on the day it was introduced and stayed there; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Rosa DeLauro introduced the bill on September 12, 2023, with 9 original cosponsors, all House Democrats [S1].
The House referred it to the Education and the Workforce Committee the same day, where no further action was recorded for the rest of the Congress [S4].
It never received a committee hearing, markup, or floor vote in the House or Senate [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers who lose wages to unpaid hours, denied overtime, or misclassification are no better off. The employers and industry groups whose business model can rely on underpaying workers avoided new damages, fines, paystub requirements, and limits on arbitration.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who shortchange workers avoided new penalties

for.name: Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 9 original cosponsors

against.name: House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Republican-controlled majority in the 118th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill during the two-year Congress

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a House Democrat — 18 of the 216 Democrats, no Republicans — and the bill never advanced in the Republican-controlled committee.

industries.industry: Employers with wage and hour violations (construction, restaurants, warehouses, home care, agriculture)
industries.note: These businesses would face up to triple damages with interest, fines as high as $110,150 per employee for willful violations, mandatory criminal referral for record falsification, and a 4-5 year window for workers to sue. Their cost of operating on stolen wages would rise sharply.

industries.industry: Arbitration and employers using mandatory arbitration agreements
industries.note: The bill overrides the Federal Arbitration Act for wage claims, so workers could not be forced into private arbitration as a condition of employment. Employers lose a tool that has kept many wage claims out of court.

industries.industry: Staffing and gig businesses relying on contractor misclassification
industries.note: Misclassification is named in the bill's findings as a form of wage theft, and the expanded damages and statute of limitations make reclassifying workers or paying them as contractors while treating them as employees costlier.

industries.industry: Payroll processing and HR compliance software
industries.note: New federal paystub and disclosure mandates would generate demand for systems that track hours, rates, and deductions across pay periods.

industries.industry: Community organizations and legal aid groups, including labor unions
industries.note: A $50 million annual grant program would fund nonprofits, unions, and legal aid to educate workers, help file claims, and partner with Labor Department enforcement.
